new_statements.translation: Drabbe §8: 'When we think it necessary to indicate which syllable is stressed, we do so by writing a grave accent on the vowel of that syllable; to which type the accentuation in this language belongs we shall not settle here.' §10: 'In all those expressions [dependency compounds such as "pig-tail"] the accent lies on the first, i.e. the determining, word. Now in Ndom one also has the same sequence with the opposite accent, and then to express a possessive relation, and ghoa ghurùb means "the tail of the pig".'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Voorhoeve's reading of Drabbe's accent-marked data, main stress falls on the last syllable of the word in most words; the primary source (Drabbe) only marks stress ad hoc with a grave accent and refuses to classify the accent system. Drabbe's page-16 Ndom forms with marks are all final-stressed (mānùmb 'flesh', krikìr 'skin', mdesàr 'laugh', unèr, anén, roàgh), but Usher's rendering of Drabbe's list also shows initial-stressed items (ˈxaraːma 'crocodile', ˈsitaxa 'arrow').
new_statements.exceptions: Voorhoeve hedges with 'generally' and 'details are not available'; Drabbe gives no rule and some of his marked forms are non-final. Drabbe §10 reports a phrase-level accent contrast: compound (accent on the first/determining word) vs possessive phrase (opposite accent) in Ndom.
new_statements.domain_note: Voorhoeve's statement is about the word ('word-final syllable'), drawn from Drabbe's citation-form wordlist. Drabbe §8 is a transcription convention covering the three languages of the article; §10 concerns two-word phrases/compounds, not word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Ndom (autonym Ndom-wer, language Ndom-bana; also Kalilam), spoken in six villages in the west of Kolopom/Frederik Hendrik (Yos Sudarso) Island; glottocode ndom1245, ISO nqm. Drabbe's 1949 data come from the Ndom villages Kariràm (Kalilam), Fatàgh, Murùba, Wétaghu, Pembrö, Sabèndar; the Susanto 2001 wordlist is from Wetau village. No dialect distinction is made in any source. Voorhoeve's Kimaghama (kima1246) and Riantana (rian1263) remarks are separate and say stress there 'seems unpredictable'.

sources.note: Segmental phonology worked from Drabbe 1949 and the Susanto 2001 survey wordlist (233 items, Wetau village); transcribes Drabbe's and Susanto's stress marks (mostly final, some initial: ˈxaraːma 'crocodile', ˈsitaxa 'arrow') and mentions vowels reduced to schwa 'in destressed positions'; no stress-placement rule stated.
